channel.title: Stimpunks.World — what changed on the street
channel.description: Every change to the rooms, the street that joins them and the campground past the treeline, newest first — including the things that are not built yet. Generated from changelog.html by tools/make-feed.py, so the page and the feed cannot disagree.

item.title: The Doom Scoop: daily news, usually bad
item.description: A new shopfront, The Doom Scoop: an ice cream parlour after closing, with the only light coming from the dipping cabinet, and a tub in the cabinet for every morning of the last week. Each tub holds what Ryan’s sources put out between five the morning before and five that morning, Mountain time: MeidasTouch for the independent news, A Closer Look, the Late Night monologues, Jimmy Kimmel Live and The Daily Show for late night, and Jason Salmon, Texas Paul, Tennessee Brando, Lawyer Oyer and Hawk’s Podcasts for the YouTubers. A week, and then it is gone. The eighth morning is not archived. It goes from here and stays on the channel that posted it. Every morning is a flavour, and the flavour is the day of the week. Nothing plays until you press it, and every scoop says how long it runs, when it went up and whose channel it is on before you do. Shorts play upright. A video whose channel will not let it be shown on another site is a door out to YouTube, and says so. Nobody here watches any of it first. A timer fills the cabinet every morning, and the page says when. The headlines are the channels’ own, word for word. Nothing is ranked or counted. Ground News and MeidasTouch News publish no feed a timer can read, so they are doors on the counter rather than tubs in the cabinet.

item.title: A wicker basket in the Faery Yurt, Helen’s first pebble, and her soundtrack
item.description: The Faery Yurt’s soundtrack is no longer coming soon. It is Helen’s own playlist, Faery Yurt’s Yarn, from her own channel: one press puts it on and it runs until you stop it, and nothing reaches YouTube before the press. The songs on it are listed underneath, with who plays them and how long each runs, as the playlist stood the day it was read. Every one was checked that day: it plays, and it may be embedded here, and the whole list was played from inside the yurt before it went up. The yurt is on Now Playing, the bill on the poster column, which noticed on its own that the room had something to play. Helen Edgar filled her basket, and asked for it to be a basket: a wicker one, drawn in her own browns with a handle over the rim, with each pebble a smooth stone sitting in it. Press a stone and it takes you where it goes. The name on a stone is a real link, so it reads and tabs like any other. The first pebble is the amethyst cave at Jupiter Artland, near Edinburgh: Anya Gallaccio’s The Light Pours Out Of Me, a 30-second video on the Yoga & Healing Fairy channel, which is not Helen’s. The line on the stone is hers, and so is the wish for a magical glimmer day. The basket’s look is the yurt’s own. The Hermitage’s basket stays a list: two rooms do not share a basket any more than they share anything else. Nothing in it moves at any setting.

item.title: Pebbles by the door, in the Hermitage and the Faery Yurt
item.description: The Solarpunk Hermitage and the Faery Yurt each have pebbles by the door. A basket of things the host has put out for anybody to take, and a bowl for leaving a pebble of your own: a line in your own words, and a link if the thing is somewhere else. It was Helen Edgar’s idea, the day she came to the Hermitage to watch a film. Anybody can see what is in a bowl; leaving a pebble takes a CB sign-on, and a pebble stays seven days, the chalkboard’s rules. A link shows its whole address, so what you read is where it goes. The privacy page says what the bowls keep. Nothing is counted: not what was taken, not what was left, not who came to the door. Leaving a pebble is the only footprint there is, and nobody has to leave one. Both baskets are empty until their hosts fill them.

item.title: The CB’s teleporter
item.description: “CH 19” on the CB’s bar is a Teleport button now. Press it and a list of every room on the street opens under the bar; type to narrow it, use the arrow keys to move, and press Enter to go. The room you are in says you are here. Escape puts it away. Teleporting is an ordinary link: it sends nothing to the channel and tells nobody where you went. The button hides while the radio is folded away, because folded sends nothing at all.

item.title: The CB can be made small
item.description: A Small button on the CB’s bar shrinks the radio to the bar and the newest message, so you can keep an eye on the channel while you watch something in a room without the radio covering the screen. It stays tucked into whichever corner you put it in, and it stays small until you press the button again, even after you move to another room. Small is still switched on: it hears the channel exactly as the full-size radio does, and a screen reader still hears what arrives. To send a message, make it full size again. Folding it away is still the way to switch it off.

item.title: The CB: rooms by #name, and a log that stays put
item.description: Name a room on the CB with a #. Type # and the start of a room’s name, like #den, pick it from the list, and everybody on the channel sees #The Den, linked, so you can ask somebody to come and find you there. It works from the keyboard: arrows to move, Enter or Tab to pick, Escape to leave your # alone. The list is every page on the street, in the street’s own order, and a new room is on it the day it opens. A room’s full address in a message, like stimpunks.world/the-den.html, is a link too. An address anywhere else stays plain words you can copy, because the channel is strangers’ words and it should not be able to send anybody off the street without their noticing. Scrolling up the channel stays where you put it. The radio used to jump back to the newest message every few seconds; now it only follows new messages when you were already at the bottom, or when you have just sent one. The radio fetches the list of rooms from this site once, the first time it listens. The privacy page says so.

item.title: The Broadsheet Broadside’s sheets are CC0
item.description: Every sheet on the press is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0, like the Stimpunks broadsides they are modelled on: print a stack and give them away, with no permission needed and no credit required. Each sheet says so on the paper, and asks for its credits to stay on it anyway. The dedication covers the sheets’ words and layout and nothing that is not ours: the typefaces keep their own licences, and Danny the Street’s name is DC Comics’. The room around the sheets stays under this street’s licence, CC BY-SA 4.0, and the licence file says which is which. Printing a sheet no longer comes out with blank pages in it when you are signed on to the CB, or when a browser extension has added something to the page.

item.title: The Broadsheet Broadside, and its first sheet
item.description: A new shopfront on the street, The Broadsheet Broadside: manifestos and mementos served across your bow. A broadsheet press in the side of a ship, printing broadsides the way the Stimpunks broadsides and whysheet.press do: one sheet, printed both sides, ink on white, on a page that fits both A4 and US Letter. Side A carries one thing you can read across a room, to pin up; side B does the work, to hand over. No. 1 is an introduction to Stimpunks.World: one street with no two rooms alike, the dial, nothing playing until you press, where to go, what stayed careful while the street got loud, and whose idea the street is. Print the page, or press the button over the sheet, and only the sheet comes out, one side to a page. The storefront is the side of a ship in the Nelson chequer, seen from a boat at the waterline, with a sheet of paper in every open port where a gun would be. No gun is drawn, nothing is fired, and nothing moves at any setting. The only light is the sun thrown back up off the sea. The ship’s name is painted in Bodoni Moda; the sheets are set in Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono, the faces the Stimpunks broadsides use. All three are read off their own records and are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. Every sheet is checked by printing it. The street’s print check now renders the press to a real PDF and refuses anything but two pages a sheet in the sheet’s own two inks; its first run found the page margins printing in Chrome’s dark canvas, which is fixed. The press’s own tool refuses a sheet that is not two sides, a claim line too long to read across a room, two sheets sharing a pair of inks, a link that does not read as its own address, and a sheet that tells its reader what they must do. A job marker, a share card, the map, and a slot on the Community Center’s service board, because the press takes ideas for its next sheet.

item.title: The Live Room, and Looming Rocks goes outdoors
item.description: A new shopfront on the street, The Live Room: a recording studio seen from the control room, over the desk, through the glass, with the red light on. It is for sessions played in a studio rather than at a gig, and it opens with three studios: Austin City Limits, a television studio with a crowd in it, and the live rooms of two radio stations, KEXP in Seattle and KCRW in Santa Monica. The desk takes suggestions. Every session is a channel strip, its name written in marker on masking tape, with where and when it was taped, whose channel it is on, a line of ours, and a play button that says how long it runs before you press it. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press. Every video was checked on its own watch page first, and every date and venue on a strip was read off that video’s own description. One Austin City Limits upload is titled a full concert and has six songs cut from it, and its strip says so before the press. The glass is two panes set out of parallel, the way studio glass is, so everything lit in the live room is drawn twice, the second time faint. The red lamp is steady at every setting and nothing in the room moves. Nobody is drawn in the live room. B612, drawn for aircraft cockpit displays, carries everything you read; Just Another Hand writes the names on the tape. Both are read off their own records and are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. Looming Rocks is for outdoor music in general now, not only for Red Rocks, and Noah Kahan’s set at Austin City Limits Music Festival 2023, in Zilker Park, is on its bill. Every act says where it was played, and the room’s tool refuses one that was not played outdoors. That rule arrived in the same message as nine Austin City Limits television tapings, which are indoors, so they went to The Live Room, whose tool refuses the opposite: a session that was not played indoors. Three of Looming Rocks’ notes had stopped being true as the bill grew, and they were fixed: one said a film was last on the bill when it was sixth, one said the oldest show was nearly forty years older than the rest when it is thirty-four, and one said nobody else on the bill had been born yet, which was not true of every band on it. A job marker, a share card, the map, a slot on the Community Center’s service board, and a place on the Now Playing poster.

item.title: Cavendish Coworking: the Hang Suites, up the stairs
item.description: Cavendish Coworking has Hang Suites, for when you just want to hang out or work on something together: the Cave, a quiet room for co-presence with no spoken chat; the Campfire, for small groups working, watching or listening together; and the Watering Hole, for come-and-go chat where random and off-topic are on-topic. Each is a Proton Meet room behind its own door. Every door says how things go in there before you knock, in the room’s own norms, and none of them has a time on it: they are drop-in rooms. Lurking with your camera and mic off is fine in all of them. They are named for David Thornburg’s caves, campfires and watering holes, the three kinds of Cavendish Space, and the room says whose they are. A note under them, on communication access: you do not need to speak to belong here.

item.title: Cavendish Coworking is Henry Cavendish’s house now, and every door in it is shut
item.description: Cavendish Coworking opened this afternoon as a glass office with every door propped wide, and that was the wrong idea of open. Ryan’s correction: transparency does not mean an open floor plan and always-open doors. It is a Georgian house now, after the one in Bedford Square where Cavendish kept his library and opened it for borrowing: green throughout, and every door a shut mahogany door in a stone case with a fanlight, a brass plate and a note saying what is behind it and when. None of them is locked. You decide whether to knock. The blinds are down, and you can see through them. That house’s mahogany blinds were lined with green transparent canvas, so the shelves show through them in the drawing. And its rules were his too: he signed the register for every book he took out of his own library. Everything about his houses is from Christa Jungnickel and Russell McCormmach’s Cavendish: The Experimental Life, credited on the page. The type is Caslon for reading as well as for the name, his century’s letter; Inter has left the street. The doors, their words and their times are unchanged, and the tool that builds them now refuses the open-plan vocabulary too.

item.title: Cavendish Coworking: every door propped open onto one of our calls
item.description: A new shopfront on the street, Cavendish Coworking: glass all the way along, and every door in it opens straight onto a Proton Meet room. Our Operations and Editorial meetings are open to the world, and until now the only way in was our Discord, which a great many people will not use. The room our events meet in is there too. No Discord, no account and nothing to install. Each door was opened as far as Proton’s guest page and no further: it asks for a name, names the room so you can check it, and lets you in with your microphone and camera off. The room says that Proton’s own terms apply over there, before you press. They are doors and not windows, and that was measured. Proton Meet only lets Proton’s own apps frame it, and this street gives no page your camera or microphone, so a call inside the page would have been a blank box. Nothing reaches Proton until you press a door. Every line on a door is our events page’s, word for word, and the times are Central as that page gives them, with the same hour worked out on your own clock underneath, in your browser. Nothing is stored or sent. A new tool builds the doors, reads the events page again every time, and refuses a line that has gone from it, a door without its room’s password, a door out of the page’s order, and the call framed in the page. Broken on purpose first; all eight caught. Named for Cavendish Space, and Henry Cavendish, who wanted to stand off to the side soaking everything in: there is a chair by the wall for anybody who would rather come in that way. Libre Caslon Display and Inter, both OFL and read off their own records, on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. A job marker, a share card, the map and a street door.

item.title: Plural Mural’s chalkboard: a note for whoever comes by next
item.description: Plural Mural has a chalkboard leaning against the foot of its wall, on the pavement and not on the paint. It is Helen Edgar’s idea, after the board at her floatation tank place: somewhere to leave a note for whoever comes by next. Anybody can read it, and only people signed on to the CB can write on it. That is what keeps it in the community’s hands. The box you write in says, above it, that the board is public. A note stays up for seven days, and the board holds thirty, so a full board loses its oldest note. The base station can rub one out sooner. There is no archive and no copy, and every read asks search engines not to keep what is on it. The privacy page changed first. It has a section on the chalkboard now, and every sentence on it that said the CB was the only thing that sends anything, or that the pass only travels when the radio listens, says what is true with a chalkboard in it. The Community Center’s account of the radio says it too, since the same sign-on writes on the board. Three small functions beside the CB’s, sharing its code: one to read the board, one to write on it and one for the base to rub out. They use the same conditional write as the channel, which was tested with fifteen people chalking at once: every note told it had gone up was on the board. Nothing a person chalks is logged, and no address is kept.

item.title: The Playhouse’s secret word: a new one every day, and the room screams
item.description: The Playhouse’s secret word changes every day now, at your own midnight, working through a rota of words out of our glossary. It said MONOTROPISM and nothing else since the street opened. The whole rota is printed under the sign, so a page with no scripts still has every word. And it does what a secret word is for: when anybody in the room says it, everybody screams. The toys talk, so when Chairy, the word clock, the telephone or the infodump says today’s word, the scream goes on the end of the sentence and the room makes a noise it makes nowhere else: five voices, not the yell button’s one. Or press SAY IT OUT LOUD on the sign. The words are the same at every setting; at MAX GLITTER the sign also jumps. Nothing flashes, and nothing is counted: no tally of screams, no streak of days. make-toys.py builds the sign and refuses a word nothing in the room ever says, because a secret word no toy can say only screams when somebody presses the sign, which is not the joke. It matches with the same pattern the script does, so the two cannot disagree about a hit. Broken on purpose first: an unsaid word, a word on the rota twice and a word that is not one word were all refused. The bit is Pee-Wee’s Playhouse’s and the sign says so on its face, and also that Groucho Marx had a secret word first, on You Bet Your Life. The first draft of the credit said Paul Reubens made it up, which is how an idea’s history gets shorter.

item.title: Community Library, L-Space and Oook: a public library, the space behind it, and a world behind that
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: the Community Library, our Library in this street’s clothes, and it opens with a celebration of the public library: free to all, a patron and not a customer, the front desk, a palace for the people, Ranganathan’s five laws, library joy, and the library economy. Our collections are laid out on the front desk. Nothing requires a card. It is a public reading room at eleven in the morning with its windows set high over the shelves and the sky in every one of them, which makes it the one room indoors on this street where you can see the sky. Behind it, through a gap in the stacks: L-Space, Terry Pratchett’s idea that every library is joined to every other by the weight of what is in them. A deep violet room where every shelf bends towards the well in the middle and the only way through is a ball of string, with the anti-library, Books of the Edges, and threads from our glossary to pull. And at the far end of the string: Oook, a Discworld homage in the Librarian’s own colours, rust and banana. The Disc on its elephants and its turtle, the rules of L-space, and why we find the Librarian of Unseen University relatable: his body changed, he found it suited the work, he declined to be changed back, and he kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the books were. He is not drawn anywhere on this site. Every quotation in the three rooms says how it was checked, and for every one the answer is: read off our Library page, not against the book. Two of them have no source on that page at all and say so where they stand. Our Library page links the 2000 graphic adaptation of Guards! Guards! for lines out of the 1989 novel; these rooms link the novel, and the tool refuses the other record. The Linda Lindas’ line and the pictures of the Librarian stay on our Library page, because a lyric and those licences are things this site cannot carry. Marcellus SC and Andika in the library, Gravitas One and Source Serif 4 in L-space, Sniglet and Libre Baskerville in Oook, all under the SIL Open Font License and on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. A job marker in each room, a share card for each, a street door, and the map now draws a room behind a room behind a room. GNU Terry Pratchett. Every page on the street now sends X-Clacks-Overhead: GNU Terry Pratchett, the clacks tradition from Going Postal that people began keeping in their websites’ headers after he died: send it on, do not log it, turn it round at the end. Oook says so, and the line in _headers says Oook depends on it. New: community-library.html, l-space.html, oook.html, data/library.json, tools/make-library.py.

item.title: Plural Mural: an end wall that will not stay one colour
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Plural Mural, an end wall with a mural on it, and then another. The street is Danny’s, and Danny repaints. The first murals are the lines of the street’s own tagline, one to a wall: queer without fear, interdependent and here, divergent and proud, living out loud, plucky pluralism, and becoming and belonging. At MAX GLITTER the wall repaints itself every three minutes, one mural dissolving into the next, and you can keep the one you like up for as long as you stay. At Gentle and Regular it holds still until you turn it over yourself, because a picture that changes without being asked is something moving on the page. Every mural is listed under the wall in words at every setting, with a button to put it up. Propose a mural of your own, in words, and the house paints it and puts it up in turn, credited to you. Nobody real is painted on the wall, nothing is voted on, and it comes down the moment you ask. It has a slot on the Community Center’s service board. Seen from across the road at golden hour, with the sun behind you and the lamppost’s shadow lying up the wall, the same over every mural. Chango and Commissioner, both under the SIL Open Font License, are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. A job marker, a share card, and a place on the map. New: plural-mural.html, mural.js, data/mural.json, tools/make-mural.py.

item.title: Now Playing: a poster column beside the Pebble Board
item.description: Street furniture on the pavement, beside the Pebble Board: a poster column with one bill pasted round it, Now Playing. Every room with something in it to press and play, on the street, behind its doors, in the campgrounds and down the road out of town, with a line about what is on there and what each one puts on first when you get there. What is on first is read off each room’s own page, every time the poster is printed: the first thing in there you can press, with its name and running time exactly as that room prints them. When a room changes what it opens with, the poster changes with it. Where a room puts on a whole playlist, the poster says so, and says what the room says about it. Beside the board and not on it, because the glass holds what our people brought each other, and a bill printed off every room is not a pebble. Nothing on the poster plays, nothing on it is counted, and there is no headliner: every room’s name is the same size, in the order you would walk to them. Screenprinted in two inks and no black, pasted on a painted iron column. Rammetto One and Instrument Sans, both under the SIL Open Font License, are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s picker. A job marker, a share card, and a place on the map. New: now-playing.html, data/now-playing.json, tools/make-now-playing.py.

item.title: A look of your own, at the Dress-Up Den
item.description: The Dopamine Dress-Up Den takes looks from our community now. Tell us what you wear, in your own words, and it goes on the peg with your name on it, or as somebody in our community: your words exactly as you give them, prints and colours picked off the rails to match, and anything you wear that is not on a rail yet drawn and hung up for anybody to wear. Words, not a photograph, because nobody’s body goes on the stand. Nothing is rated, and it comes down the moment you ask. It has a slot on the Community Center’s service board, beside everything else the street takes in, held to the room’s own words so the two cannot come to disagree. Taking something back now lists your look as well. Changed: dopamine-dress-up-den.html, data/community.json, community-center.html.

item.title: Dopamine Dress-Up Den: try it on, and nothing comes in a size
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Dopamine Dress-Up Den, a boutique for dopamine dressing. The room and its name are Helen Edgar’s idea. Put an outfit together on a wooden valet stand out of the rails — something on your head, something over the top, something underneath, the bottom half, your feet, and a feather boa or a long scarf — in any print and any colours: florals, big blocks of colour, patchwork, stripes, polka dots, gingham, moons and stars, sequins, or plain. Or press Surprise me. The rails start from Ryan’s wardrobe: Thai fisherman pants, button-down shirts, a haori over the top and beanies and slouchy beanies in every colour there is. Then Helen’s cardigans and flowing dresses, and then the full show, with a big wig, a velvet cape, a sequin gown, platform boots and the boa, for anybody in our community who wants all of it at once. Each of those is a look off the peg you can put on the stand and change. And Crocs, on Ryan’s ask the same day. Every garment says how it feels and how it goes on and comes off, because our glossary defines dopamine dressing as colours, textures and styles, and Ryan wears his pants for sensory and comfort reasons first. The fastenings follow his own field guide page on dressing: every jacket says how you get out of it, and the knot on fisherman pants is not accessible to everybody, so every other bottom half does up without one. Nobody’s body is drawn. The clothes hang on a stand rather than on a paper doll, because a doll is one shape, one skin and one gender handed to everybody who walks in. Nothing comes in a size, no rail is for men or for women, and nothing is rated, kept or sent; the copy button puts what is on the stand on your own clipboard. Black is a colour in there too. Every rail comes in all black, because our Dress Codes entry has a school that banned black clothing on the grounds of mental health, and a room that told people colour was the cure would be that dress code with a nicer name. The room also makes no claim about brain chemistry: dopamine is in the name because that is what people call it. The light is the only light on the street that has been taken apart. The sun comes in the front window white, which lets every colour on the rails look like itself, and a crystal hanging in the window throws small rainbows on the lavender wall. At MAX GLITTER they drift a little as it turns, and nothing flashes or sparkles on its own at any setting. The dial never takes anything off the rails. Two new typefaces: DynaPuff, by Toshi Omagari and Jennifer Daniel, for the sign and the headings, and Plus Jakarta Sans, by Tokotype, for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. Changed: dopamine-dress-up-den.html, dressup.js, data/dressup.json and tools/make-dressup.py (all new), og/dopamine-dress-up-den.png (new), fonts/, index.html, love.css (§52 is the new room; small screens and print are §53 and §54 now), data/quests.json, liner-notes.html, the Foundry and the Mopery’s picker, and the map.

item.title: A placemat and some crayons at The Small Hours
item.description: Every table at The Small Hours now has a paper placemat and a sleeve of crayons. Pick a crayon, then press a shape to colour it in, or switch to scribbling and draw wherever you like, over the lines included. The wax has the paper’s tooth in it, so it looks like crayon rather than paint. Every part can be coloured in by name from a list under the placemat, with a keyboard or a screen reader, and each name says what colour that part is now. Scribbling is the one thing that needs a pointer or a finger. Nothing on it is kept. A fresh placemat throws the old one away, and leaving does the same. Take it home saves a picture of it to your own device and sends it nowhere; the house rule saying nothing is kept now says so about the placemat too. tools/make-small-hours.py refuses the room’s script if it ever starts storing, sending or reading the clock. With scripts off, the placemat is still there to print out and colour in with real crayons. Changed: small-hours.html, small-hours.js, data/small-hours.json, tools/make-small-hours.py, love.css (§2 has the paper and the crayons; §44 has the placemat), tools/check-contrast.py, liner-notes.html, README.md, llms.txt, CLAUDE.md.

item.title: A documentary’s title at the campfire, corrected
item.description: Corrected: on the Solarpunk Hermitage’s campfire listing and in the liner notes, the title of Coastal Seas showed three stray characters where “World’s” has its apostrophe. YouTube’s own page had it right; our copy of the title had been read in the wrong encoding. It is YouTube’s title again, and tools/make-hermitage.py now refuses text read that way anywhere in the room’s data.

item.title: The community service board
item.description: The Community Center has a community service board: a painted steel sorter on the wall by the desk, with a slot for every room on the street that takes something in from our community. A photograph for the Polaroid Wall in Enid’s Room, a collection for The Collection Collection, a yell for the Playhouse, a pebble for the Pebble Board, a quotation for the Zibaldone, a page for the zine, your samefoods, something to watch or listen to for the rooms with a screen or a playlist, a poem for the Doomscroll, an idea for Your Room, and an idea for a new shop, pitch or turning. Two slots are for when something is wrong: one for anything we got wrong, including anything you cannot read, reach or press, and one for taking back anything with you in it. That comes down when you say so, and coming down means gone. Nothing on the board sends anything. Every slot says how its own room already asks to be reached and points at the room’s own words. The CB is not a way in: it forgets at midnight and everybody on it can read it. A slot repeats another room’s terms, so it is held to them. tools/make-community.py reads each room’s published page and refuses if the room has stopped saying what its slot says, so the board cannot keep promising something a room has changed. It also refuses a form, a route no room offers, and any hint of a score: nothing on the board counts who gave what. The rooms with a playlist or a screen now say so themselves. Dance, Punks, Vital Plant Living and Club Chronic take song suggestions, and Laughingstock, the Lightbulb Picture House, Looming Rocks, Black Leather Lagoon and the Hermitage’s campfire take recommendations, each in its own words, and the board is held to every one of those sentences the same way. The Collection Collection already said how to put something in a cabinet, so its slot points there now. item.title: The Community Center, and the CB
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: the Community Center, a painted block hall at ten in the morning with the blinds half open, the chairs stacked against the wall and a radio on the front desk. It holds the house norms for the CB and points at our covenant. The CB is a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio. Sign on at the front desk with a handle and this week’s password, and the radio rides along in the bottom right corner of every page until the password changes or you sign off. Drag it by its bar, or press Move and use the arrow keys. It keeps the latest ten messages and deletes everything at midnight, Colorado time. There are no alerts: no sounds, no notifications, no badges, and nothing saved up for when you come back. Open, it listens; folded away or in another tab, it sends nothing. It is the first thing on this site that sends anything, so the privacy page changed first. What the channel keeps, what it never keeps (no IP address, no list of who signed on, nothing written into a log), where it lives and who can read it are all written out there. The security policy now lets a page talk to this site and nowhere else (connect-src’self’), and the radio’s script is never downloaded by anybody who has not signed on. The radio stays out of the Healing Checkpoint, which promises it writes nothing down about you. In the rooms where it does go, a few promises that had been about the whole page now say what they were always about: the Arcade’s cabinets, Quill Drift, the Guild’s stamps, the Repeater’s open line, and the headset and the stage in Dance, Punks and Looming Rocks. Two new typefaces: Varela Round, by Joe Prince, for the letterboard, and Radio Canada, by Charles Daoud, Coppers and Brasses, Alexandre Saumier Demers and Jacques Le Bailly, for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker. item.title: Vital Plant Living: build your own bowl, and everything in it touches
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Vital Plant Living, a plant-based kitchen. Build your own bowl or wrap out of Ryan’s own pantry, the list he cooks from at home, in his three steps — base, texture, flavour — or start from one of the combos on the board, each standing on a flavour base from somewhere in the world that is off his list: the Cajun holy trinity, a sofrito, a mirepoix, garlic, ginger and scallion, and the rest. Copy your bowl or wrap to the clipboard and take it shopping: everything in it comes out one per line, under the pantry’s own section names. Nothing is stored and nothing is sent anywhere; closing the page empties the bowl. Everything in the room is drawn cut through the middle, the way a cook sketches a dish to show what is in it: your bowl, wrap or sandwich changes as you tick, with every layer sitting on the one under it and the sauce running into the rice. It is Samefood Cafe the other way up, a few doors along, where nothing on a plate touches anything, and the house rules send anybody who needs their food apart there by name. The pots on the shelf over the counter are cut open too, and every one of them is something in the pantry. The room was briefed as Ital Plant Livity, and it says where the name went. Both words are Rastafari’s, and Rastafari has been a big influence on Ryan; but this kitchen cooks with salt, MSG and things out of packets, which many people who keep Ital do not, and how Ital is kept varies from person to person and is not ours to settle. So the name over the door is the plain-English one, the menu never calls a dish Ital, and the room says all of that near the top rather than in a footnote. The stereo plays Ryan’s playlist of songs about food, most of them reggae and dancehall, and nothing plays until you press play. Every song is listed with who made it, how long it runs and who uploaded it, because several were put up by fans rather than by the musicians. The menu makes no claims. Nothing on it is called authentic, nothing is good or bad for you, and nothing is counted; where a combo is thinking about a dish usually made with something the pantry does not keep, it says so. tools/make-vital.py refuses a combo that brings in anything the pantry does not keep, and refuses all of that vocabulary in the room’s own voice. Two new typefaces: Bagel Fat One, by Kyungwon Kim and JAMO, for the kitchen’s name and its headings, and Be Vietnam Pro, by Lâm Bảo, Tony Le and ViệtAnh Nguyễn, for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. item.title: The Map: the whole street in white card, and a Where am I? on every page
item.description: New street furniture by the front door: The Map, the whole street as a model in white card on a cutting mat. Every shopfront stands where it stands, on the side of the road it falls on, with the rooms behind rooms standing behind them; the garden’s gate is halfway down; the campground’s field is off the top of the board past the treeline and the road out of town is off the bottom past the last streetlight. Every building, tent, sign and tag on it goes to the place it stands for. Every page now has a Where am I? at its foot, next to the liner notes. It opens the map at the page you were on, with a flag on it saying you came from there. Nothing is stored and no script is involved: the page’s own name is the address of its place on the model. Nothing on the model is painted. Every room here has its own light and its own colours, and a map that painted them all would be telling you they belonged to one set. So it is one white card, and each room is left to be itself when you get there. Nothing on it was placed by hand. The model is built out of the street itself — the front page’s row of shopfronts in the order they stand, the campground’s board and the road’s signs — so it grows when the street does, and a new room cannot open without going up on it, because the build refuses until it has. On a phone both sides of the road are kept, because which side a room is on is the point of a map. Two new typefaces: Architects Daughter, by Kimberly Geswein, for the lettering on the model, and Albert Sans, by Andreas Rasmussen, for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. item.title: The Collection Collection: the house brings the furniture, the light is theirs
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: The Collection Collection, a dark gallery of our people’s collections. Every collection stands in a cabinet of its own under a lamp of its own, and no two lamps are alike: a daylight lamp over Ryan’s pens, paper and ink, because a warm bulb lies about the colour of an ink, and a strip light inside his perfume cupboard’s door, because light spoils perfume. A cabinet with nothing in it yet stands with its lamp off, and its label is exactly as easy to read as a lit one. Ryan’s pens, paper and ink are in, under their daylight lamp, and his perfume cupboard is still dark, waiting for its photographs. Norah and her husband’s leather swatches and stamping tools, Chelsea’s house plants and Helen’s books and rocks each have a cabinet with their name on it, say that Ryan relayed them, and stay empty until they send something. Their lamps are theirs to choose. The house describes every photograph so that nobody has to. Writing a title, a description and a caption for every picture is work, and work is what stops people sending a picture at all. So Claude writes them, looking at each photograph, and every cabinet says so on its label. It describes only what it can see and never names a maker or a model from what a thing looks like; an owner’s own words win wherever they give any. This is the opposite of the polaroid wall on purpose: a description of a person is theirs to write, and a description of a pen is not a description of anybody. Nothing is counted, priced, valued or ranked, and nobody asks how many. Every photograph is stripped before it reaches the site. A new tool takes phone photographs in, turns them the right way up, removes the location and every other scrap of metadata a phone writes, makes them smaller without cropping them, and leaves a record that stops the room building until somebody has described each one and looked at the whole frame for a person or an address. The room’s own tool refuses a photograph that still carries any metadata, a filter on any photograph, and two cabinets with the same lamp. The photographs are not under this site’s Creative Commons licence, so that anything can still come down when its owner says so. Two new typefaces: Gloock, by Duarte Pinto, for the room’s name and every label’s heading, and Hanken Grotesk, by Alfredo Marco Pradil and Hanken Design Co., for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. item.title: The feed keeps a busy day in order
item.description: Entries from the same day used to arrive in any order. Every one of them carried the same time, noon, so a reader had nothing to sort them by. On a day with more than ten, stimpunks.org’s feeds page showed ten of them in an order of its own and left out the newest. Now the top entry of a day keeps noon and each one under it is a minute earlier, so every reader lists them in the same order as this page. The dates are still true. The minutes are only the order, and not a claim about when anything was written. Nothing reappears as new. Each entry keeps the identifier it was published under. item.title: The street is Stimpunks.World now
item.description: The site lives at stimpunks.world, and it is called Stimpunks.World. We had been calling it Stimpunks World for a while, as it grew past one street into rooms behind rooms, a campground past the treeline and a road out of town, so the domain was registered to match and the name moved with it: every page title, the feed, the favicon, the share cards, and the wordmark on the front door, whose pink second line now says.world. Every old link still works. stimpunks.love stays ours and sends you, page for page, to the same place here. The certificate covers both. Your feed reader should not see anything twice. Each changelog entry keeps the identifier it was published under, so moving house did not turn a week of entries back into news. The older entries below still say stimpunks.love where that was where the street was at the time. We did not go back and rewrite them to match. item.title: Samefood Cafe: your favourite, the way you have it
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Samefood Cafe, for samefoods and safe foods, and for understanding food aversion rather than correcting it. The kitchen knows its regulars: it keeps what each of them has, the way they have it, and is ready for the day their samefood changes with the season. The menu is whatever the regulars ask for, a dish goes on when somebody asks, and nothing comes off because somebody else got bored of it. Samefoods have seasons, and the room says so. Nothing touches unless you want it to, and that is the room. Separation is offered, never imposed: the house’s divided plate keeps different foods apart and the ramekins keep red things off everything, and a bowl is one person’s dish, the way they eat it, touching as much as they like — some of us need everything apart and some of us do not mind at all. It is drawn from directly above the table, under one even light that is the same at every hour, so every object sits in its own soft ring of shade. Every plate on the page is the same plate — the menu, the book and every tray — which is Covenstead’s mismatched china turned inside out, one door along. The menu is three entries from our glossary, Samefood, Safe food and Food aversion, each with one short line from somebody who has written about it: C.L. Lynch at NeuroClastic, Kari Burroughs Kraakevik at Thinking Person’s Guide to Autism, and Matthew Broberg-Moffitt. Two were read against their own pages; the two from the book could not be, and the room says so beside them. On the counter: Color Taste Texture, by Matthew Broberg-Moffitt, with its details read off Open Library’s record, and a way to find it in a library as well as a shop. The regulars’ samefoods are on trays of their own, written down exactly as they were given and not tidied, sorted, ranked or added up. Ryan’s, Helen’s and Ronan’s are the first, each with a bowl of their samefood of the moment — ramen with fresh green onions, pesto pasta, chicken nuggets; more are being collected in our community’s Discord. Every list comes down when its person asks, and every food drawn on the plate in the window is off one of them. We default to structure, separation and predictability, and every guest is accommodated individually — never regarded as fussy, picky or too much, just quietly and professionally accommodated. Nobody’s way imposes on anybody else’s plate: Ronan has red things in a ramekin of their own, so his ketchup comes that way, and the room’s tool holds his food, and nobody else’s, to it. Two new typefaces: Fredoka for the café’s name and headings, and Inclusive Sans, drawn so that no letter can be taken for another, for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. item.title: The Small Hours gets a jukebox, and one song printed in full
item.description: The Small Hours plays both of Josephmooon’s albums, So Far So Good and Hand in Heaven, every track, streamed from the band’s own site and hosted nowhere here. Josephmooon is the music project made for the lyrics of Ronan Boren, a Stimpunk, and Stimpunks helped produce it. Every button says how long its song runs before the press, measured off the file itself; only one song plays at a time; and the two album buttons say how many songs and how long before they start several. “Up All Night” is on the counter with its words printed in full, a song about Autistic insomnia, with its credits: Ronan Boren, all lyrics; Bill Paige, vocals and guitar; Ronnie Nice, guitars, keyboards, bass, drums and programming; Ian Nice, piano, keyboards and backing vocals. That is permission rather than quotation: every other room quotes a line or two of a song or none, and this is the one song on the street published whole, because Stimpunks holds permission to distribute it and its lyrics. make-small-hours.py refuses a lyric without a written-down permission, the words are excluded from this site’s licence in LICENSE, and the agent skill’s “no lyrics” line now names the one exception. A recording from somebody else’s server needed its own origin list. love-embed.js has an AUDIO_ORIGINS array beside its frame list and builds the players; make-csp.py reads it into a new media-src, path and all, because without one the policy falls back to 'self' and the jukebox would be a row of buttons that press and play nothing. The privacy page lists the band’s site among the services a press can reach. item.title: Four new turnings off The Outskirts, each lit a way the road had not been
item.description: Turning 04, Dance, Punks: a silent disco on an old airstrip, lit by nothing but the headsets. Three channels that are our Dance, Punks playlist started in three places — the room says so, and never calls it shuffle — and tuning is silent while the headset is off. The volume is on the player, so the loudness this whole street hands the visitor is handed to every dancer. The three channel colours are held at least 1.5 to 1 apart in brightness so they stay three headsets in greyscale, and nothing on the runway strobes or moves at any setting. Each channel’s opening song was pressed and heard starting where it says. Turning 05, The Small Hours: an all-night diner seen lit from the dark car park, for bodies that keep other hours. Crip time in Alison Kafer’s words, a clock with no hands, a menu with no prices, and no sleep advice anywhere, for a reason one of its quotations gives. The sign does not read your clock. The crayons passage in our Sleep entry is Sarah Kurchak’s, and this room nearly credited it to somebody else from memory: our entry links the book without naming its author, so every author here was resolved against a library record. Turning 06, The Repeater: a radio mast on the ridge at the far end of the road, where everything is a silhouette against the glow of everybody else’s light. Our Shared-Signal Space entry is its argument, a log confirms every kind of contact and counts none, and a line you can leave open is a quiet noise made in your browser that sends nothing and listens to nothing. The Autistic Rhizome was first credited here to Helen Edgar alone; our own entry shows DGH Neurodivergent Consultancy named it, and both are credited now. That article’s own address now serves a holding page, so the room links our entry instead. Turning 07, Nothing For Sale: a free market in a lay-by, lit by a ring of cars that pulled up nose-in and left their headlights on, so everything in the middle throws one shadow for every car. Solidarity, not charity; tables of free things of ours, each checked against its own page; no proof of need; nothing counted. Our mutual aid grants are pointed to rather than laid out, because they have an application and a waiting list and a table would promise otherwise. A new tool for each, and every refusal in them was broken on purpose and fired. Two were wrong on their first run and were narrowed rather than excepted: the disco’s animation check refused its own section’s comment describing the refusal, and the lay-by’s charity check refused the room’s sentence explaining what charity is. check-jukebox.py had not been able to run since Laughingstock opened. That room’s data file carries acts as well as sets, the branch for acts came first, and the comics were read as videos with no artist, so the whole run refused before checking anything. sets is tested first now, and the disco’s three opening songs are in its lists. The diner’s jukebox is not, because none of it is on YouTube. Syncopate is under the Apache License 2.0, not the OFL, and the first draft of two credits said otherwise; the pulled record caught it. Looming Rocks’ board, description and house rules still said six concerts when the bill has ten, and say whole concerts now rather than a number. item.title: The Lightbulb Picture House: every screening is a relaxed screening
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: The Lightbulb Picture House, a picture house showing films about autism, ADHD and neurodiversity, most of them made by the people they are about. It is named for Thriving Autistic’s short film Lightbulb Moments: Being Autistic, which is on its first screen. Two screens, both our own playlists: Animated Introductions to Autism, ADHD, and Neurodiversity and More on Autism, ADHD, and Neurodiversity. Each plays whole and runs until you stop it, and every film on them was checked on its own watch page before it went up. The rack has a card for every film on Screen One, in the order it plays: who made it, where it was published, how long it runs, a line of ours about it written from the film rather than from its title, and what is in it, said before you press — a panic attack, a bullying scene, jokes about suicide, a sponsor segment. Where one of our own pages already carries the film or the idea, the card links to it. Every screening is a relaxed screening. The house lights stay up, the captions come on by default, and you can move, stim, sit on the floor, come in late and leave early. The drawing of the auditorium is lit all over, with a floor cushion in the aisle and a pair of ear defenders on a seat. Nothing in the building is blue. A lightbulb theater lit blue would be Light It Up Blue, the awareness campaign autistic people have spent years refusing, and Amy Sequenzia says why on the page. The bulbs are warm, the ornament over the screen is the gold infinity, and tools/make-picture-house.py reads the room’s palette and refuses a blue — along with the vocabulary of awareness in our own voice, a film with no note of what is in it, and a pronoun for any maker, because none of the films says what theirs are. Two new typefaces: Limelight, an Art Deco fascia face, for the name and the headings, and Outfit for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker. At MAX GLITTER the popcorn in the second row pops; no bulb ever flickers. item.title: Laughingstock: a comedy club where only the comics stand in the light
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Laughingstock, a comedy club down a ramp rather than a flight of stairs. It leads with our own writing from the Campfire Learn Together Being Disabled Can Be Pretty Funny: comedy is a form of knowledge, and disabled comics take the stage on their own terms, in their own voice, controlling the frame. The stage is our own Disabled Comedy playlist, put on whole and running until you stop it, and beside it is the bill — every set on that playlist, one press each, the comics named on every one and the runtime said before you press. Josh Blue, Tina Friml, AJ Wilkerson, Benny Feldman, Steve Way, Ahren Belisle and Fiona Cauley. Nothing plays until you press play. The light comes from behind you, and the only thing that stands in it is what the comics said. One follow spot throws a hard-edged pool onto a brick wall, and each of Josh Blue’s and Tina Friml’s lines stands in an oval of that light with their name under it. Everything of ours — the write-up, our notes, the house rules — is out in the dark with the audience. Nobody is drawn on the stage: a mic, a stool, a glass of water, and a ramp up to it. House rules: no cover and no two-drink minimum, nobody in the front row made part of the act without asking, talk to the comic and not to whoever came in with them, bombing is allowed, nobody is called brave, and nobody headlines. tools/make-laughingstock.py refuses the vocabulary of inspiration and of ranking in the room’s own voice, and skips the comics’ own lines, so that “I suffer from people” is allowed to say suffer. Two new typefaces: Yellowtail, a sign-writer’s script, for the neon and the comics’ names, and Bricolage Grotesque for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. At MAX GLITTER the water on the stool goes sparkling; the neon never flickers. item.title: Dead Tired Society: the big lights off, the door ajar, and nobody in the light
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Dead Tired Society, peer support by and for people in burnout and people on the far side of it. The name is a play on Dead Poets Society, and the name is the only thing taken from the film — no line, no scene, no character. It is a borrowed room after hours with the big lights off and the door left ajar, and the only light is the corridor’s, lying across the floor through the gap. Every word on the page stays in the shade on purpose: masking is performing under a light, and this is the room where nothing has to. Nobody is drawn in the picture of it, because nobody in there is on display. By the door there is a row of pegs for what people carried in — masking, minority stress, epistemic injustice, justice sensitivity, moral injury and neuronormativity, and more named further along the wall. Each says what is hanging on it, gives one short line from somebody who has written about it, credited to them, and adds a line of ours. Every line was read off our own glossary, and where a source was named only by title or initials the authors were looked up rather than guessed. Standing orders nobody is standing for, and a talking piece you can pass, because passing is a whole turn. What you type into it goes nowhere and is not kept. What it will not do is written on the page and enforced by its tool: no advice nobody asked for, no tips, nobody praised for resilience, no timeline, nothing counted, nobody at the front. It is not a meeting and says so, and points at our community and at mutual aid. Near the top, a line for anybody whose night is worse than tired, pointing at our Help and Coping pages. Two new typefaces: Sorts Mill Goudy for the society’s name, and Lexend for everything you read, which was drawn to ease reading fatigue. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves and in the Mopery’s font picker, with their designers named. The desk keeps its credits and the dial; the way back to the street is the link at the top of the page, as it is in every room. Changed: adventurers-guild.html.

item.title: Lighter pictures, where that is measurably true
item.description: Fifty-six of the street’s JPEGs are WebP now, and the pictures on those pages weigh about 29% less — 2.4MB across the scans, prints, engravings, photographs and thumbnails. The biggest single waste went with it: the Pebble Board’s video thumbnails were stored 1280 pixels wide and are never drawn wider than 170, and they are 512 now, which still covers a phone screen at three times density. Twenty-four stayed JPEG, each for a reason written down. Every file was converted at the lowest quality that measured as faithful to its source, and swapped only if that saved at least a tenth. Most of Doré’s and Tenniel’s engravings did not clear that bar: fine hatching is the one thing lossy formats are worst at, and at the same fidelity WebP was no smaller than the JPEG, sometimes larger. Converting them anyway would have meant a heavier file or a softer engraving, chosen for the format’s sake. data/webp.json holds every decision and its numbers. The first attempt measured the wrong thing and was undone. It compared colour as well as detail, and WebP always stores colour at half resolution, as most JPEGs do — so on small, bright thumbnails it concluded no quality was good enough and left the oversized ones exactly as they were. It had deleted JPEGs under that rule, so everything went back to the last commit and ran again measuring detail, which is what the eye looks for. Nothing about the pages changed but the files. WebP goes into the same image tags, so no room’s layout moved; AVIF was often smaller still, but serving it safely means wrapping every picture in a new element, and at least one room’s layout depends on its images not being wrapped. The share cards and icons stay PNG, because link previews and home screens do not all read anything else. Every picture on the affected pages was loaded and checked afterwards, and the photographs still carry no location or device data. Changed: images in raven/, oracle/, alice/, pebbles/ and photos/, data/mopery.json, data/oracle.json, data/rabbit-hole.json, data/pebble-board.json, data/webp.json (new), the pages those generators write, og/oracle-deck.png, tools/make-webp.py (new), tools/make-og.py, README.md, CLAUDE.md.

item.title: Honest sitemap dates, three videos unsquashed, and a consent date for every voice
item.description: The sitemap stopped saying the whole street changed every time it was rebuilt. Every page’s lastmod used to be the day the sitemap was generated, which tells a crawler that everything is new whether or not anything is — the exact mistake the specification names. Each page’s date is now the day of the last commit that touched it, read out of the repository’s history, and the tool refuses to run where there is no history to read rather than guessing. Three videos on the Pebble Board were squashed. Every play button takes the shape its player will have, and three of the board’s videos are older and four-by-three: their thumbnails were being stretched to fill a sixteen-by-nine box, every face in them a third wider than it is. They are fitted now, with the board’s own night either side, which is what the player shows once you press it. Not cropped: those frames have no bars to cut, and taking a quarter off a music video to fill a box would be the same fault the other way round. Every recorded voice on the street now has a consent date, the readings in Hear Queer Here included. The yells and the Faery Yurt’s recordings always carried one; the readings did not, which is why the privacy page had to word its promise around them. They were agreed to on the day each recording landed, and that date is now read off the commit that added each file rather than typed. make-readings.py refuses a recording without one, as the other two audio tools do, and the privacy page makes the plain promise it could not make before. Changed: sitemap.xml, tools/make-sitemap.py, love.css (the Pebble Board’s section), data/readings.json, tools/make-readings.py, privacy.html.

item.title: Structured data, and a note for any agent reading the street
item.description: Every page describes itself in JSON-LD, the format search engines and agents treat as fact. Everything in it comes out of that page’s own head — its title, its description, its address — so it cannot say anything the page does not. The publisher is marked with the same identifier Star Stuff uses, so two of our sites describe one Stimpunks Foundation rather than two. The licence is on the site, not on each page, because the photographs of people are excluded from it. The missing-address page gets none: it has no address to describe. There is a skill for agents, at /.well-known/agent-skills/stimpunks-love/SKILL.md: how to read, quote and cite this site. It says where the indexes are, why the site gives no count of its rooms and what to do if you need one, that the rooms are different on purpose, that two of them must not be summarised as advice or a fortune, and what the licence covers — including that the photographs are not to be reused. The counting check reads it, so it obeys the site’s own rule. /.well-known/api-catalog lists every machine-readable resource (RFC 9727), and every response now points at it. It uses only link relations that are actually registered, which is why the sitemap and the skill are not in it under relations they do not have — Star Stuff found out the hard way and published the correction. Both files are generated: the skill’s sha256 is computed from its bytes on every run, and the catalogue refuses to name a file that does not exist. Both refusals were tested by breaking them. Changed: every page’s head, llms.txt, _headers,.well-known/api-catalog,.well-known/agent-skills/ (new), tools/structured.py, tools/make-structured.py and tools/make-agent-files.py (new), tools/make-foundry.py, tools/make-sitemap.py, tools/check-counts.py, README.md, CLAUDE.md.

item.title: Every page signs off, in its own voice, with a way back to the top
item.description: Every page now ends with the same short line: back to the top, the liner notes, Your Room, the changelog, the privacy page, the feed, and whose street this is. Somebody looking for how to leave, who made this, or what happens to them finds it in the same place wherever they are, which is what the privacy page in particular needed. It is not the front page’s footer, on purpose. The street ends on its chalk pavement and keeps it; our own notes have said since the Guild opened that the street’s footer reaching into a room would be the one piece of the street’s look in a world that has its own. So the line brings no colour, no typeface and no ground: it is set in whatever the room already uses, the way the job markers are, and reads as the room signing off. The pavement takes its links from the same list, so the two cannot disagree. Back to top is a plain link, and it moves the keyboard too. It jumps rather than scrolls, at every dial setting, and the next Tab after it lands on the skip link at the top of the page rather than on whatever followed the line. It works with scripts off. One room needed its own. The Zibaldone’s link colour is a rubric red chosen for paper, and the line lies on the dark desk below the sheets — 1.07 and 1.74 there. It takes the laid paper’s own colours on the desk now. Every other room’s links already cleared their own floor. It does not print. A link on paper goes nowhere and “Back to top” at the foot of a sheet is false — and it pushed issue #2 of the zine onto a second sheet the day it arrived, which check-print.py caught. Changed: every page, love.css §4, the Zibaldone’s section and Print, tools/signoff.py and tools/make-signoff.py (new), tools/make-foundry.py, tools/check-contrast.py, tools/check-print.py, README.md, CLAUDE.md.

item.title: A privacy page, which is short because there is very little to say
item.description: The privacy page says what this site knows about you, and all of it. No cookies on any response; two settings in your own browser, both things you asked it to remember; nothing from any other service until you press play, with each player’s own policy linked; and the ordinary logs our host keeps. Netlify’s analytics is not switched on. It names who publishes the site, where to write, what your rights are, and that every change to it will be dated here. Every sentence on it was checked against the site rather than written from what a privacy page usually says. The storage keys were read out of the scripts, the absence of cookies off live responses, the embed services out of the one list the site frames, and each outside policy link was requested. One draft sentence did not survive: it said every recording on the street had a dated consent record, and the readings in Hear Queer Here, read by the people who made that room, do not carry one. The sentence says what is true instead. It is linked from the front door’s footer, the liner notes, the Polaroid Wall and the security policy, is in the sitemap, and has a share card. It carries no job marker: the page somebody reads to find out what happens to them is not a stop on a walking tour. Changed: privacy.html (new), index.html, liner-notes.html, polaroids.html, SECURITY.md, tools/make-sitemap.py, tools/make-guild.py.

item.title: Sentences that had stopped being true, somewhere to report a hole, and a real favicon.ico
item.description: The site was still counting its rooms in places the counting check could not see. The Playhouse opened by giving its own number on the street, Your Room said it was linked beside a number of others, the Arcade’s description gave its number too, and the favicon’s own source said its stripes were the rooms, one each. check-counts.py looked only for a number in front of a noun; it now also catches the number after one, and the total left hanging at the end of a sentence with the noun understood. Its first run refused a count of tilted leaves in our own notes, and the pattern was narrowed rather than the sentence excepted. It reads the favicon, netlify.toml and SECURITY.md now as well. llms.txt said every typeface was under the SIL Open Font License. Four are Apache 2.0, which the Foundry found out by reading each family’s own record. The line is generated from that record now instead of typed, so it names both licences and will name a third if one ever arrives. A comment in netlify.toml said the domain redirect was still switched off. It was switched on on 2026-09-19. There is a way to report a security hole. /.well-known/security.txt, per RFC 9116, and a SECURITY.md saying what this site actually is and what is worth reporting. The contact is GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting, switched on for this repository today, because an issue on a public repository discloses a report the moment it is filed. make-security.py writes the file and refuses from thirty days before its expiry date, because a lapsed security.txt is invalid rather than merely old. /favicon.ico exists. Browsers and crawlers ask for it whatever a page’s head says, and until today every one of those requests got the missing-address page. There is an Apple touch icon, and the manifest carries 192, 512 and maskable icons for installs. Every one is rendered from favicon.svg by make-icons.py, at each size directly rather than scaled down, and the manifest’s list is written by the same tool, so an icon cannot be declared without being drawn. The security header upgrades anything insecure it meets. Nothing on the site loads over plain http today; upgrade-insecure-requests is there so that a link pasted into a room tomorrow gets upgraded instead of blocked as mixed content. The Faery Yurt’s two photographs reserve their room before they load. Helen Edgar gave a standing yes today to maintenance that changes nothing a visitor can see, and this is the first of it: both photographs were measured before and after, at desktop and phone width, and render identically. Anything that changes how her room looks is still hers to decide, and the liner notes say so. Changed: playhouse.html, your-room.html, arcade.html, faery-yurt.html, favicon.svg, every page’s head, love.css comments, netlify.toml, _headers, site.webmanifest, SECURITY.md (new),.well-known/security.txt (new), favicon.ico, apple-touch-icon.png and three manifest icons (new), tools/make-icons.py and tools/make-security.py (new), tools/check-counts.py, tools/make-sitemap.py, tools/make-csp.py, tools/make-guild.py, tools/make-foundry.py, tools/check-contrast.py, README.md, CLAUDE.md.

item.title: A focus ring you can see in every room, and the headings, links, tables and pictures a screen reader walks
item.description: On fourteen pages the focus ring was very nearly invisible somewhere. The ring is 4px of yellow, chosen for a street that is near-black, and it is right there. The pale rooms were never given one of their own: on the Guild’s manila it measured 1.01, and it was no better than 1.31 on the Garden, Covenstead, both zines, the Zibaldone’s paper and the Hermitage’s daylight, on the white cards in Pink Pony Club and the Playhouse, on Club Chronic’s flyers, on the Pebble Board’s cards, on the Den’s track cards and on the pebbling cabinet’s overcast shore. Somebody moving through those rooms by keyboard was moving an indicator nobody could see. Each room chose its own, which is the point. There is no new street-wide ring: every room that needed one takes the ink it already writes in, set in its own section beside its own link colour — the clerk’s ink, the loam, the tea-dark brown, photocopier black — and where a room has a dark panel inside a pale one, or a pale card on a dark floor, the panel decides. The Hermitage needed four, because its cave is velvet, its television is glass and its coffee table is cedar. Every one clears 3:1 against every ground it lands on, and the dial keeps its yellow in every room because it is always a dark box. Nothing had ever measured a focus ring, so there is a tool that does. check-focus.py renders every page, focuses every control and measures the ring against what it is drawn on. It measures a gradient at every one of its stops and passes only the worst, and it was wrong twice before it was right: it first counted the dark room behind the Latibulum’s plaster as a ground the ring might stand on, then composited the Den’s three layers of shag onto the room instead of onto each other. Both were fixed in the tool, and the Guild’s ring was removed on purpose to prove it still fails. Three pages skipped a heading level, and all three were generated. Looming Rocks’ running order and the Hermitage’s campfire went from h2 to h4, and the Doomscroll’s headlines were h3 with each poem’s title as an h2 inside them — upside down. Fixed in the generators, and every heading’s computed style was compared before and after, so nothing moved on the page. check-headings.py refuses a skipped level now. Links that did not say where they went. The Latibulum’s dictionary link said here; it says whose dictionary now. Club Chronic’s twelve flyers each said Go, which a screen reader moving from link to link hears as twelve identical words — the flyer still says Go, and the rest of the sentence is there for the ear. And one card on the Pebble Board was a link with no name at all. Every table has a caption and every column header says it is one. Twenty-two tables across the liner notes, the photograph promises and Your Room. The captions are visually hidden, because each table already sits under a heading saying the same thing to anybody who can see it. Pictures reserve their room before they arrive. Sixty-nine images on the Pebble Board, in the Mopery, in the Rabbit Hole and on Enid’s wall had no width or height, so the page jumped as each one landed. The generators read the size off the file’s own header now, through one small shared reader checked against every image in the repository, and every picture was measured before and after so that none of them changed shape. The two photographs in the Faery Yurt are Helen Edgar’s markup and were left alone. Changed: love.css §3 and the section of every room that needed its own ring, pink-pony-club.html, zine-table.html, zine-issue-2.html, latibulum.html, liner-notes.html, polaroids.html, your-room.html, the pages the generators below rebuild, tools/check-focus.py (new), tools/check-headings.py (new), tools/imgsize.py (new), tools/make-looming.py, tools/make-hermitage.py, tools/make-doomscroll.py, tools/make-club.py, tools/make-pebble-board.py, tools/make-mopery.py, tools/make-rabbit-hole.py, tools/make-polaroids.py, tools/make-og.py, README.md.

item.title: An address that is not on the street, and the Gentle default when storage is blocked
item.description: A missing address has a page now. Until today any URL nobody built got Netlify’s own teal “Page not found”, with the right status and no way back to the street. 404.html is fog: a house-number plate on a post with no house behind it, rooftops going back into the air until they are gone, and the ways out — the street, the garden for our other sites, a person to tell. It still sends a 404, it is marked noindex, and every path on it starts with a slash because it answers at any depth. Fog is lit from everywhere, and nothing else on this street is. Every other world is lit from somewhere or from nowhere; fog scatters light until it arrives from every side at once, so nothing casts a shadow, nothing has a lit face, and the only thing that tells near from far is how pale a thing has gone. That is what keeps it off the Adventurer’s Guild, which is lit from nowhere and has no depth at all. Nothing moves in it at any setting. It has no share card, no job marker and no place in the sitemap, and each tool says why by name. It has no address of its own to unfurl, post a job at or list. make-og.py, make-guild.py and make-sitemap.py exempt it explicitly, so every other page still refuses to ship without all three. One sentence on it was false in its first draft and a measurement caught it. It said a capital letter or a stray space was enough to land here. Netlify folds both back to the right page; what actually lands here is a dropped letter, or the full stop or bracket a link picks up when it is copied off the end of a sentence. The dev server is no guide to this, because the disk it serves from ignores case. The render checkers were looking at a different page from the one that ships. A root-absolute path loaded from a file:// probe points at the root of the disk, so check-contrast-live.py and check-gentle.py would have measured the 404 unstyled — and an unstyled page passes everything. Both probes now resolve those paths against the repository, and check-ids.py stopped counting /love.js and love.js as two scripts. The dial’s default ignored a device asking for less motion whenever storage was blocked. The snippet every page runs before first paint read the stored setting first and fell back to Regular if that threw, which some private windows do — so a visitor who had asked for reduced motion got the louder version, which is the precise failure the dial exists to prevent. It reads the device’s preference first now and only lets a stored choice override it. The CSP hash moved with it, and make-foundry.py reads the snippet off the front page instead of keeping its own copy, which it would have put back on its next run. The web manifest was still counting rooms. Its description said how many there were, which is the sentence check-counts.py exists to refuse — and it had never looked at the manifest, which is shown when the site is installed. It is on the tool’s list now, read as code rather than prose, because a JSON file is nothing but quoted strings and skipping quotation there skips the whole file. Changed: 404.html (new), love.css §2 and §39 (Small screens and Print are §40 and §41 now), every page’s pre-paint snippet, _headers, site.webmanifest, tools/check-counts.py, tools/check-contrast.py, tools/check-contrast-live.py, tools/check-gentle.py, tools/check-ids.py, tools/check-classes.py, tools/make-foundry.py, tools/make-guild.py, tools/make-og.py, tools/make-sitemap.py.

item.title: Looming Rocks Amphitheatre, and a stage lit from the ground up
item.description: Turning 03 in The Outskirts is a venue. Looming Rocks Amphitheatre is an open-air stage at the foot of two enormous rock faces: six full concerts, a lighting desk that walks the bill without loading anything, and a great deal of stone that was here long before the stage was. It earns that road rather than the campsite — crowds, volume and staying out late is exactly what the road is for. The light is thrown upward and nothing else on this street does that. Floods stand on the ground and point up the rock, so a face is brightest at its foot and goes dark towards the top, and there is nothing overhead at all. That is the exact inverse of Sithen one turning back, lit by a full moon from directly above, and of the Lagoon two turnings back, flat frontal light across water at eye level. Three rooms on one road, three directions of light, and vertical was the one nobody had taken. And what glows is not the lamp. The lichen fluoresces — it takes light you cannot see and gives back light you can — which is emission rather than reflection, and the third kind of transmitted light here after Swaying Sweetgrass (through grass) and The Feed (through a mask). The lamps are violet; what comes back is cyan-green. That green is the pair to watch: the Lagoon’s acid is a yellow-green one turning along the same road, and the two are far apart in blue on purpose. The stage is the Hermitage’s set on a rock face, and it keeps that set’s promises. While the stage is dark, tuning is silent and nothing is fetched; once something is playing, tuning changes the picture. The desk names the act it is about to move to and how long that runs before the press, which matters more here than at the campfire: these are full concerts, the shortest nearly an hour and the longest over two. looming.js is a separate file from hermitage.js on purpose — the two sets look alike and are not the same object, and a shared widget would be the harmonising instinct arriving through a script tag. The running order is a <details> and opens and closes with no script at all. A refusal was copied from the herbarium and did not survive the move. That room catches a guessed Latin binomial with a shape test — one capitalised word, one lowercase word — which works on a page of short labels and, run over prose, matches the start of nearly every sentence. Its first run here refused “Rocks that”, “Once something” and “Ferrell sings”. Excepting those phrases would have been the mistake this repo has already written down three times, so the pattern was narrowed structurally instead: sentence starts are ignored, and it only reads sentences that are about lichen at all. Verified in both directions — a real binomial in a lichen sentence is caught; a band name in a note is not. The room stopped explaining which half of itself was invented. A first draft had a section headed what the rocks are, and which half of that is made up. Ryan cut it: this is a street named after a genderqueer, shape-shifting road, and a disclaimer explaining that the sentient rocks are fiction is a page apologising for being the thing it is. His own intro is the room’s opening now. What still needs saying is the part about somebody else’s property, and that is a different job living in the credits. The real venue is credited as somebody else’s.
